events.excerpt: South Korea said on Friday that Google had met the safety rules for sending detailed maps of the country overseas. This brings Google closer to offering full navigation services after 19 years of disputes with the South Korean government. South Korea’s Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport said on Friday that a team of government officials and outside experts had confirmed Google followed the security rules, according to the Korea Herald. The team checked whether Google had met the conditions set on February 27, when South Korea allowed it to send highly detailed maps of the country overseas. These maps use a 1:5,000 scale, meaning they show much more detail than regular maps. Google submitted its final report on November 4. As part of the changes, Google removed information showing exact locations in South Korea from Google Maps and Google Earth. This applies to both the websites and the Android and iPhone apps. Google also added a system that blocks app updates if they include location details that are not allowed. This is meant to stop the removed information from appearing again. events.excerpt: Unocoin says crypto left one of its wallets even though it froze its BitGo account in its latest update on the exploit it suffered. Unicoin thinks a backup recovery path in BitGo’s (NYSE: BTGO) multisignature wallets was used to move its funds, but it does not know who the perpetrator is. How did crypto leave a wallet that was frozen? Unocoin asked BitGo to freeze its company accounts on November 6 after it spotted suspicious activity. Its blog says the freezes began at 11:24 UTC for Fireblocks and 11:29 UTC for BitGo. Both custodians confirmed the freezes, and no losses were found at that point. However, on November 13, Unocoin said its money was moved out of the wallet that BitGo confirmed was frozen. Unocoin says BitGo’s multisignature wallets have a backup path that is meant to let a client reach funds even if BitGo goes offline. Unocoin says this path “appears to have been exploited” and that it is now checking how it was reached and used. BitGo’s own documents point fingers at its clients instead. Its Wallet Recovery Wizard lets clients take assets out of their wallets “without BitGo.” It uses the user key and the backup key to move funds to a new address. events.excerpt: Bitcoin Magazine Digital Credit: Comparing The Six Bitcoin Preferred Stocks Digital credit is an emerging asset class that transforms corporate Bitcoin balance sheets into income producing securities. Strategy pioneered the market with five perpetual preferred equity instruments: STRK, STRF, STRD, STRC, and STRE (the first four are listed in the U.S.). Strive subsequently introduced SATA and SATS, bringing the category to six U.S. instruments across two issuers. These securities offer investors preferred equity (read: credit-like) exposure to companies whose balance sheets are dominated by Bitcoin. Their perpetual structure means investors principally rely on recurring dividends and the continued financial strength of the issuer. Unlike term debt, there is no maturation date at which the full principal is ever paid back. Evaluating digital credit requires examining four characteristics: creditworthiness, investor protections, liquidity, and dividend profile. This article explains all four dimensions and then offers a ranking for the six digital credit instruments along these lines. None of this should be taken as investment advice—it is only a systematic framework for analyzing digital credit. 1. I want to talk about AI hacking. There are three aspects: people hacking AI systems, people using AI to hack other systems, and AIs hacking systems on their own, not even maliciously. The last two matter more than the first. The third is the weirdest and potentially the most destabilizing. I started writing about this in 2021 and in my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind . Back then I said it was mostly still science fiction, but not stupid science fiction. We’re seeing it more and more, especially in the past year. The trends I’m describing don’t require a major breakthrough in AI. They’re starting to happen now, and they’ll happen more often as AIs get better at autonomous problem-solving. And it will involve far more than computer code. AI will hack all sorts of social, economic and political systems. It will find vulnerabilities and exploit them. This is a difference in kind, not just degree. We’re not ready for it, and we need to think about the implications now. events.excerpt: Doing board level diagnosis on a PCB is hardly black magic, but some PCBs are definitely more daunting than others. The Socket LGA 1851 mainboard that [Fix the Pixel] got in for repair being one of the harder cases due to the sheer size and complexity. Adding to the excitement was having to purchase a used CPU for it off eBay to even test the board and work through the boot-up sequence to find the culprit. A basic understanding of how these mainboards power up and verify that they can move on to the next phase is essential here, starting with the power rails. Although the culprit turned out to be a single missing 5.1 Ohm resistor on an SPI clock line, you still have to reason your way through the diagnosis. For this mainboard the boardview was fortunately available, but that still doesn’t make it easy to spot components that have quietly left the chat. With the CPU and RAM installed the board doesn’t bother to boot up, with the VRM controller for the CPU’s power phases showing its enable pin to stay low. Going down the list of conditions for this pin to be pulled high the culprit was eventually found, when the PCH – the board’s chipset – never reading the BIOS chip. Checking the SPI lines on the mainboard near the BIOS chip quickly showed the knocked-off resistor on the SPI clock
events.headline: Fixing a Dead Socket LGA 1851 Mainboard with a Resistor
